samples.summary: The new CLI login `nonce` is a bearer-grade binding secret carried in a URL query string that the request logger records verbatim (redaction covers headers only)
samples.evidence: `packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:46` sends the secret as a query param: `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}&nonce=${encodeURIComponent(nonce)}`. On the backend, pino-http's request serializer logs `url: req.url` (`app.module.ts:68`) — the full path *with* query string — and the `redact.paths` list (`app.module.ts:76-83`) only censors `req.headers.authorization`, `req.headers.cookie` and `res.headers["set-cookie"]`; nothing strips query parameters. `customLogLevel` maps this 302 GET to `debug`, so it is silent at default `info`, but any deployment with `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, any 4xx on that route (→ `warn`, logged at info), or any reverse proxy / CDN access log in front of the backend captures the nonce together with the callback port, both in the same line. Attack: read one log line, then from any page in the victim's browser navigate to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>&state=<leaked-nonce>` inside the 30s window (`login.ts:257-265`) — `nonceMatches` at `login.ts:206` passes and the CLI redeems the attacker's code, which is precisely the RFC 8252 §8.9 outcome the change claims to prevent. The whole mitigation collapses to the secrecy of a query parameter that the repo logs unredacted.

samples.summary: The loopback-injection defence is client-side only; the backend still completes an unprotected CLI flow for any client that omits `nonce`
samples.evidence: `github-auth.guard.ts:34-38` treats `nonce` as optional (`typeof nonce === 'string' && nonce.length > 0 && nonce.length <= MAX_NONCE_LENGTH ? nonce : undefined`), and `auth.controller.ts:130-132` emits `stateEcho = ''` when `state.nonce` is falsy, then still mints a code and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=...` with no `state`. So `POST /auth/cli/exchange` remains reachable via an entirely unbound flow: any already-installed CLI (or a CLI-shaped client) that does not send a nonce gets the pre-change, fully vulnerable behaviour, and the server has no switch to refuse it. A nonce longer than 128 chars is also silently downgraded to `undefined` rather than rejected, so a client that believes it is protected gets an unbound redirect back. Note the new CLI does fail closed (`login.ts:206` rejects a missing `state`), so this is a fleet/compat exposure rather than a bypass of the new gate — but the docs (`docs/design/cli.md:196-205`) describe the binding as unconditional.
searchedFor: searched for any server-side rejection of nonce-less cli state

samples.summary: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` has no proof-of-possession: the nonce now available server-side is not required to redeem the code
samples.evidence: `auth.controller.ts:155-168` accepts `{ code }` alone, with no authentication and no binding to the flow that started it (`consumeCode` returns the userId for anyone presenting the code). The code travels in a URL — `res.redirect('http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=...')` at `auth.controller.ts:133-135` — so it lands in the browser's address bar, history, and (per `app.module.ts:68`) potentially in access logs. Within the 60s TTL (`cli-auth.store.ts:66`) anyone who observes it can exchange it for a full access+refresh token pair; the throttle is 10/min but a single successful read is enough. The change stores a per-login nonce that would serve exactly as a PKCE-style verifier here (require `{ code, nonce }` and compare against the state entry), but the exchange was left unbound.
searchedFor: grep for any nonce/csrf use at exchange time

samples.summary: CLI loopback callback server does not check `req.method`, contradicting the documented "accepts only GET /callback"
samples.evidence: The request handler at `login.ts:187-210` inspects only `url.pathname`, `code` and `state`; `req.method` is never read. `docs/design/cli.md:191-192` states the local server "binds to `127.0.0.1` only, accepts only `GET /callback`". A cross-origin `POST` (a simple request with `Content-Type: text/plain`, so no CORS preflight) therefore also reaches the code path that resolves `callbackResolve(code)` at `login.ts:251-254`. The nonce gate still stands in front of it, so this is surface widening rather than a live bypass, but the documented restriction is not implemented.

samples.summary: Loopback callback server accepts any `Host` header — no DNS-rebinding defence on the port the comment calls the thing "the nonce gate is the only thing guarding"
samples.evidence: `login.ts:188` builds the URL with a hard-coded base (`new URL(req.url ?? '/', 'http://127.0.0.1')`) and never validates the incoming `Host` header against `127.0.0.1`/`localhost`. A DNS-rebinding attacker (hostname resolving to 127.0.0.1) can therefore reach the listener as a *same-origin* peer for the duration of the 30s window and read responses, not just fire blind navigations. The success HTML at `login.ts:212-249` does not contain the code, so I could not complete a chain to code exfiltration on its own — but combined with any nonce leak (see the query-string logging finding) it turns a blind injection into an interactive one. RFC 8252 loopback receivers are expected to reject non-loopback Host values.
searchedFor: grep for 'host' header handling in packages/cli/src
grep for other loopback servers / startCallbackServer call sites

samples.summary: Unauthenticated `GET /auth/github?mode=cli` inserts up to 128 bytes of attacker-chosen data into an unbounded in-memory map whose cleanup is O(n) per insert
samples.evidence: `github-auth.guard.ts:31-39` calls `createState` on every unauthenticated `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<valid>`, and `cli-auth.store.ts:34-41` inserts into `this.states` with a 5-minute TTL and then runs `cleanup()` (`cli-auth.store.ts:81-85`), which scans the entire `states` and `codes` maps on every insert — quadratic work as the map grows. The change makes each entry carry up to `MAX_NONCE_LENGTH = 128` chars of caller-supplied string (`github-auth.guard.ts:6,34-38`). `githubAuth` carries no route-level `@Throttle` (unlike `githubAuthCallback` and `cliExchange`), so only the global 120 req/min/IP bucket (`app.module.ts:98`) applies; a distributed source can inflate the map. Pre-existing map, but this change adds the attacker-controlled variable-length payload.

samples.summary: The CLI prints the OAuth URL containing the login nonce to stderr, putting the binding secret into terminal scrollback and CI logs
samples.evidence: `login.ts:46-48` builds `oauthUrl` including `nonce=<32 random bytes>` and then `console.error('Opening browser: ' + oauthUrl)`. The URL is deliberately printed for copy-paste in headless environments, which means the secret that solely guards the loopback port (`login.ts:206`) is emitted to stderr and will be captured by CI job logs, tmux/screen scrollback, and screen shares. `docs/design/cli.md:204-205` asserts the nonce "never leaves the user's machine and the backend except through their own browser", which understates this path. Consider printing a redacted URL alongside the full one, or shortening the accept window.

finding.evidence: `packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:46` sends the secret as a query param: `${server}/auth/github?mode=cli&port=${port}&nonce=${encodeURIComponent(nonce)}`. On the backend, pino-http's request serializer logs `url: req.url` (`app.module.ts:68`) — the full path *with* query string — and the `redact.paths` list (`app.module.ts:76-83`) only censors `req.headers.authorization`, `req.headers.cookie` and `res.headers["set-cookie"]`; nothing strips query parameters. `customLogLevel` maps this 302 GET to `debug`, so it is silent at default `info`, but any deployment with `LOG_LEVEL=debug`, any 4xx on that route (→ `warn`, logged at info), or any reverse proxy / CDN access log in front of the backend captures the nonce together with the callback port, both in the same line. Attack: read one log line, then from any page in the victim's browser navigate to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker-code>&state=<leaked-nonce>` inside the 30s window (`login.ts:257-265`) — `nonceMatches` at `login.ts:206` passes and the CLI redeems the attacker's code, which is precisely the RFC 8252 §8.9 outcome the change claims to prevent. verdict.reason: Every claimed element checks out in the repository. The CLI puts a 32-byte binding secret in a URL query string (packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:42,46). The backend pino-http request serializer logs `url: req.url` verbatim (packages/backend/src/app.module.ts:68), which includes the query string, and `redact.paths` (app.module.ts:77-81) covers only `req.headers.authorization`, `req.headers.cookie` and `res.headers["set-cookie"]` — nothing touches `req.url`. Those header paths are in fact already inert, because the custom serializer (app.module.ts:65-71) never emits `headers` and pino applies redaction after serialization, which confirms query-string redaction is genuinely absent rather than handled elsewhere. While a 302 GET maps to `debug` and is silent at the default `info` level (app.module.ts:30,47-59), `res.statusCode >= 400` maps to `warn` and IS emitted at default level; `/auth/github` is subject to the global ThrottlerGuard (app.module.ts:120-123), so a 429/4xx on that URL writes the nonce plus callback port to the log in a stock production deployment, as does any LOG_LEVEL=debug deployment or fronting proxy access log. The exploit chain completes: login.ts:206 `nonceMatches` is the sole gate on the localhost listener (see the comment at login.ts:171), it accepts any caller echoing the correct `state`, the `code` is taken straight from the query (login.ts:196-201), resolved (login.ts:251-254) and redeemed (login.ts:66-70) within the 30s window (login.ts:257-265) — i.e. the RFC 8252 §8.9 authorization-code injection the nonce was added to prevent. Backend plumbing confirms the nonce arrives as a query param and is echoed as `state` (github-auth.guard.ts:26; auth.controller.ts:130-131). This is in-lane for Security as logged-secret / sensitive-data exposure (CWE-532) with an auth-binding bypass as the consequence; no refutation ground applies: the code is present as described, no guard strips query parameters, and the lens explicitly covers logged credentials. Exploitation needs log-read or proxy-log access, which justifies `major` rather than `critical`, matching the reviewer's rating.

finding.summary: CLI auth code is still not bound to the client (no PKCE); the nonce only gates the local listener, so an intercepted code is fully redeemable
finding.evidence: The change cites RFC 8252 §8.9, whose actual prescription for the loopback-redirect code-injection problem is PKCE. What landed is a `state` echo checked only inside the CLI's own listener (`packages/cli/src/commands/login.ts:206`). The code itself remains an unbound bearer: `POST /auth/cli/exchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) takes `{ code }` with no authentication, no `code_verifier`, and no reference to the nonce — `consumeCode` looks up only the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71). Attack: anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL — from the victim's browser history/URL bar (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` is a real navigation), a browser extension, a shared/kiosk machine, or an intercepting proxy — POSTs it to /auth/cli/exchange and receives the victim's `accessToken` + `refreshToken`. The nonce does nothing here because the CLI listener is not in the path. Grepped the whole repo for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge: zero hits. Severity is 'major' rather than 'critical' because it needs code interception, and confidence is low because I could not demonstrate a concrete interception channel in this codebase.

verdict.reason: Verified independently: the CLI authorization code is bound to nothing but a userId, and no PKCE-equivalent client binding exists anywhere in the repo. CodeEntry holds only { userId, expiresAt } (cli-auth.store.ts:17-20) and consumeCode keys solely on the code (cli-auth.store.ts:71-79). POST /auth/cli/exchange (auth.controller.ts:152-168) carries no @UseGuards, only @Throttle, and its DTO permits exactly one field, code (auth.dto.ts:3-7); app.module.ts:119-124 registers only ThrottlerGuard globally, so nothing else authenticates the call. The nonce exists only on StateEntry (cli-auth.store.ts:13) and is used solely to append &state= to the loopback redirect (auth.controller.ts:130-134); it is never attached to the minted code, so it cannot be re-presented at exchange. The matching check lives in the CLI's own listener (login.ts:206), outside the exchange path, and the nonce is optional at the start endpoint (github-auth.guard.ts:34-37), so codes can be minted with no state echo at all. A repo-wide grep of packages/ for pkce/code_verifier/code_challenge/verifier/challenge/S256 yields only unrelated test-harness hits (frontend/scripts/verify-hunt-oracles.mjs:351, frontend/src/app/harness/hunt/bridge.ts:301). Anyone who observes the code within its 60s TTL (cli-auth.store.ts:66) can POST it and receive the victim's accessToken + refreshToken. Single-use consumption and the short TTL are mitigations, not client binding, so already-guarded does not apply; the issue sits in the crypto/auth lane and is a real major weakness, not out of scope.
